name: Botulinum toxin A
lead: Botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A) is a protein made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum that blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, temporarily relaxing the muscle it is injected into. In very small, purified amounts it is among the most widely used cosmetic treatments in the world; commercial products include Botox Cosmetic, Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify and Letybo [1][2].

People use it to look smoother, fresher or more defined. Injected into the small muscles that pull the skin into creases, it softens dynamic wrinkles in the upper third of the face: frown lines between the brows, forehead lines and crow's feet. The effect typically appears within three to five days and lasts around two to four months for frown lines, in some patients six months or longer [1]. Clinicians also describe using it to slim the lower face by treating the masseter muscle, to lift or shape the brows, and as one component of combined 'liquid facelift' approaches with fillers and skin boosters [3][4][6].

The chain from toxin to appearance is short: relaxed muscle, less skin folding, smoother-looking skin and, with masseter treatment, a narrower-looking jaw as the muscle gradually reduces in activity. Research includes randomized trials of cosmetic combinations, a large meta-analysis of upper-face safety, and trials in jaw clenching and facial pain, alongside decades of therapeutic studies for migraine, spasticity, dystonia and bladder disorders [5][6][9][12].

Because every product carries a boxed warning about distant spread of toxin effect and treatment is delivered by clinicians, descriptions of practice in this article rest on clinical literature, labels and regulatory history rather than on do-it-yourself instructions [2].

paras: Injection into the muscles beneath facial wrinkles relaxes them, smoothing the overlying skin [1]. The US label for Daxxify, for instance, is indicated for temporary improvement in the appearance of moderate to severe glabellar lines associated with corrugator or procerus activity in adults [2]. Wikipedia's article on facial rejuvenation lists neuromodulators such as Botox among non-surgical options alongside chemical peels, dermal fillers and laser resurfacing, favoured for lower cost and shorter recovery than surgery, and cites American Society of Plastic Surgeons data that 2013 saw a then-record 6.3 million botulinum toxin type A injections in the US [38].

Typical treatment areas are the glabellar complex between the brows, the forehead and the lateral canthal area around the eyes. A 2025 randomized, double-blind split-face trial in 25 women tested onabotulinumtoxinA together with a hyaluronic acid skin booster (Skinvive) for moderate and severe canthal lines, evaluating efficacy and durability [6]. A registered phase 4 study tested variable doses of Dysport across the full face in sun-induced wrinkles (90 participants) [7]. International consensus recommendations address aesthetic use of a ready-to-use abobotulinumtoxinA product [8]. Wikipedia's coverage of the cosmetic literature also lists reports on periorbital wrinkles, gummy smile and facial asymmetry [1].

Facial contouring uses include injection of the masseter and combination approaches in so-called liquid facelifts, described in a 2024 review [4]. The masseter is the main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw; because the toxin reduces its activity, practitioners and patients describe treatment as a way to soften a square or bulky lower face, and the same injections are studied for jaw clenching [9]. A 2020 randomized placebo-controlled trial in 30 people injected the masseter in sleep bruxism, with polysomnography before and at 4 and 12 weeks [9]. Studies in masticatory muscle pain and bruxism-related myalgia compared botulinum toxin with other approaches [10][11].
Neuromodulators are often discussed together with hyaluronic acid products and skin boosters in the same session, a pairing the periorbital split-face trial examined directly [6][4].

Wikipedia lists spasticity (cerebral palsy, stroke, spinal cord injury), cervical and other dystonias, strabismus, blepharospasm, hyperhidrosis, overactive bladder and migraine; FDA approved prophylaxis of chronic migraine in 2010, while episodic migraine is not approved [1]. The PREEMPT 2 trial reported on onabotulinumtoxinA in chronic migraine [12]. Reviews cover overactive bladder, gastrointestinal uses, facial palsy synkinesis and pre-operative use for ventral hernia repair [13][14][15][16]. A 1991 New England Journal of Medicine review surveyed therapeutic uses in the early years of the field [40].

subs.h: From sausage poisoning to a therapeutic idea
paras: Botulism was first linked to food in southern Germany: a 1793 outbreak at Wildbad, Württemberg, followed blood sausage, and from 1817 to 1822 the physician Justinus Kerner published detailed descriptions of the symptoms and proposed that the toxin might treat disorders of an overactive nervous system, the first therapeutic suggestion [1]. The word botulism, from the Latin for sausage, was coined in 1870, and Émile van Ermengem identified the causative bacterium after a 1895 funeral outbreak in Ellezelles, Belgium [1]. Types A and B were identified in 1919, and mid-twentieth-century laboratory work, including military research, established that the toxin blocks acetylcholine release [1].

The ophthalmologist Alan B. Scott of the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute in San Francisco sought an injectable alternative to eye muscle surgery for strabismus. After monkey studies showed targeted, long-lasting paralysis, he treated the first strabismus patients in 1977 and named the product Oculinum [1][35]. In 1986 his micro-manufacturer could not obtain product liability insurance and supply stopped; US blepharospasm patients travelled to Canadian eye centres for about four months [1][39]. The FDA approved the drug in December 1989 for strabismus and blepharospasm under the Orphan Drug Act [1][39]. Allergan acquired the product in 1991 and began using the Botox trademark [35][37].

Cosmetic use was discovered by chance during ophthalmic use [35]. Wikipedia credits the Sacramento plastic surgeon Richard Clark with the first described aesthetic use, correcting forehead asymmetry after a facelift, reported in 1989, and J.D. and J.A. Carruthers with a 1992 glabellar-line study in which 16 of 17 follow-up participants improved [1]. A 1994 report described treating periorbital wrinkles [1]. Cosmetic use was widespread well before the FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for moderate-to-severe glabellar lines in 2002 [1][39].

In 2008 and 2009 the FDA reviewed reports of toxin spread, issued warnings and added boxed warnings; the products were given the established names onabotulinumtoxinA, abobotulinumtoxinA and rimabotulinumtoxinB, and Health Canada issued a similar warning in 2009 [1]. The 2010 approval for chronic migraine followed [1]. Competing cosmetic neurotoxins include Dysport, Xeomin and Jeuveau; the FDA approved daxibotulinumtoxinA (Daxxify) for glabellar lines in September 2022 and letibotulinumtoxinA (Letybo) in February 2024 [1][2]. Allergan, maker of Botox, was bought by AbbVie in a deal announced in June 2019 at $63 billion and closed on 8 May 2020; Botox had annual sales of nearly $4 billion in 2019 [37]. Wikipedia reports that in the UK the number of professionals administering Botox reached 19,701 in 2025, a 437 percent increase since 2023 [1].

The toxin enters motor nerve terminals and cleaves SNAP-25, a protein needed to dock and release acetylcholine vesicles; recovery occurs gradually as nerve terminals recover from the cleavage and new endings form [2]. Earlier work showed that tetanus and botulinum-B toxins block neurotransmitter release by cleaving synaptobrevin [17]. A 2025 review covers the molecular architecture and mechanism [18]. Potency units are not interchangeable between products [2].
Literature reviews discuss immunogenicity of BoNT-A across clinical and cosmetic treatment and the factors involved in nonresponse in aesthetics [19][20].

Safety: a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of glabellar and forehead injections included 24 studies with 4,268 injection sessions and 1,234 placebos, and reported a 16 percent overall complication rate, headache, local skin reactions and facial neuromuscular symptoms being frequent. Complication odds with abobotulinumtoxin were higher than with placebo (odds ratio 1.62) [5].
Wrinkles: the periorbital split-face trial of onabotulinumtoxinA with Skinvive and the full-face Dysport dose study are the main cosmetic trials in the reference set [6][7].

Bruxism and jaw pain: a randomized placebo-controlled trial in sleep bruxism, a randomized pilot in temporomandibular masticatory pain, and a prospective comparison with dry needling, drugs and manual therapy for bruxism myalgia [9][10][11].
Melasma: a 2025 split-face randomized study examined botulinum toxin A in melasma [21].

Other registered studies cover chronic neck and back pain (60), oromandibular dystonia (240), hypertrophic scar itch (60), Raynaud's phenomenon (24), vaginismus (40) and vulvodynia (5) [22][23][24][25][26][27]. A topical botulinum eyedrop study on palpebral fissure was terminated after 2 participants [28].

Mood and emotion: small trials and a 2021 meta-analysis of onabotulinumtoxinA in unipolar depression suggest benefit, with heterogeneous results, according to Wikipedia; the leading hypothesis is the facial feedback hypothesis [1]. An fMRI study by Hennenlotter and colleagues found reduced amygdala and brainstem activity during angry expressions two weeks after frown-muscle injections, and Havas and colleagues (2010) found slower reading of angry and sad sentences after treatment [36].

The US label has a boxed warning that effects of all botulinum toxin products may spread from the injection area, with symptoms reported hours to weeks after injection; swallowing and breathing difficulties can be life-threatening and deaths have been reported, and risk is probably greatest in children treated for spasticity (an unapproved use for Daxxify) [2]. The label also lists hypersensitivity, cardiovascular adverse reactions, increased compromise in pre-existing neuromuscular disorders, dysphagia and ophthalmic adverse reactions [2]. There are no data on use in pregnant women, and animal studies showed fetal growth effects at maternally toxic doses [2].

Wikipedia lists facial weakness, swallowing difficulty, headache, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions among cosmetic-use effects, and notes that double vision from spread has been reported in at least three cosmetic cases; serious effects are more often reported with therapeutic dosing [1]. In the cosmetic upper-face meta-analysis, the authors note that increasing popularity is met with limited regulation, potentially posing risk to patient safety [5]. A 2025 case report described iatrogenic botulism after injection for palmar hyperhidrosis [1]. Reports in the literature also describe botulinum toxin as a potential biological weapon, with consensus public-health recommendations published in JAMA in 2001 [29].

Cosmetic botulinum toxin is one of the most widely recognised aesthetic treatments, and the brand name Botox is commonly used generically. The market is dominated by Allergan's Botox, with a growing field of competitors and ready-to-use formulations [8][37]. Treatment is often combined with fillers and skin boosters as part of a broader aesthetic routine [4][38].

On T Nation, mentions are mostly casual: members joke about celebrities whose faces look expressionless or 'frozen' after Botox, and about injections alongside other cosmetic procedures [30][31][32]. One member reports considering Botox for a facial concern [33]. Protocol discussion is rare in the forum material, so descriptions of practice here rest on clinical sources.

lore.intro: In forum material, botulinum toxin appears mostly in casual comments about celebrities and cosmetic procedures rather than in how-to threads [30][31][32]. Wider cultural debate concerns frozen-looking faces, jaw slimming and whether treatment affects mood.

claims.claim: Botox leaves faces frozen and unable to express emotion
claims.believers: T Nation posters remark that celebrities who use it can no longer move parts of their face, such as the upper lip, or have lost expressiveness [30][34].
claims.experts: Facial neuromuscular symptoms are among frequently reported treatment-related complications in a 2022 meta-analysis, which reported an overall complication rate of 16 percent [5]. Effects are temporary and typically last two to four months for glabellar lines [1].

claims.claim: Botox smooths dynamic wrinkles in the upper face
claims.believers: Commenters assume it is the standard injectable for lines and discuss it alongside other cosmetic procedures [31][33].
claims.experts: Product labels are indicated for temporary improvement of glabellar lines, and Wikipedia describes it as relatively safe and effective for wrinkles in the upper third of the face [1][2].

claims.claim: Botulinum toxin can slim the jaw or treat clenching
claims.believers: Jaw contouring is discussed in aesthetic circles as a use of masseter injections.
claims.experts: Randomized trials have studied masseter injection in sleep bruxism and masticatory pain, rather than cosmetic slimming outcomes [9][10][11].

claims.claim: Masseter injections give a slimmer, more defined jaw
claims.believers: Aesthetic practitioners describe lower-face slimming as a use of masseter treatment, alongside brow shaping [3][4].
claims.experts: Randomized trials of masseter injection have mainly studied bruxism and muscle pain; published trials in the reference set do not measure cosmetic jaw outcomes [9][10][11].

claims.claim: Botox can change mood by blocking frowning
claims.believers: Supporters of the facial feedback hypothesis say frowning feeds emotional experience, so weakening the frown muscle may lift mood [36].
claims.experts: Imaging and reading-time studies reported altered emotion processing, and a 2021 meta-analysis of depression trials showed heterogeneous results; a 2019 meta-analysis found only small effects of facial feedback overall [1][36].

claims.claim: Results last about three to four months and need repeating
claims.believers: Cosmetic clinics present maintenance sessions as routine, and combining toxin with fillers or skin boosters is common [4][6].
claims.experts: Wikipedia gives a typical duration of two to four months for frown lines, with some patients longer [1]; reviews discuss immunogenicity and nonresponse in repeat treatment [19][20].

claims.claim: Toxin can drift away from the injection site
claims.believers: Public discussion of 'frozen' or drooping faces reflects concern that toxin affects unintended muscles [30][34].
claims.experts: The label's boxed warning states that toxin effects may spread from the injection area, and cosmetic meta-analysis lists neuromuscular symptoms among frequent complications [2][5].

angle.text: Weakening the muscles that crease the skin softens frown lines, forehead lines and crow's feet for a few months at a time. Treating the masseter is used by clinicians for lower-face contouring. Results fade and are renewed with repeat sessions.
